card.hook: Here's a museum you can photograph without buying a ticket or even going inside. The Pedro de Osma Museum in Barranco sits right there, waiting for its close-up.
card.stand_here: Head to Avenida Pedro de Osma and stand about 20 m south-west of the museum, right at the phone icon on the map. Face north-east and the building will be straight ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the whole frontage. If it won't all fit, tap 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x or more (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the building with the vertical lines so the walls stand up straight.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the walls. It's often quieter then too.
card.selfie_here: Flip to the front camera, tap 0.5x if your phone has it, and step back so the building sits over your shoulder. Hold the phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the building from outside. If you want to go in, check the official site first, as access to museums can be ticketed or restricted.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole frontage, then find a doorway, a window or a decorative detail for a second picture that looks like it came from a different day.
card.good_to_know: The Pedro de Osma Museum is in the Barranco district and makes a good first stop on this map. Its entrance, walls and any garden greenery give clear shapes, textures and colour that show up well on a phone screen. There's room to step a little left or right to change your angle.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to Avenida Pedro de Osma and stand about 20 m south-west of the museum, right at the phone icon on the map. Face north-east and the building will be straight ahead of you.

card.hook: Picture a slim wooden bridge floating above a ravine road, with old Barranco houses on either side. Couples used to meet here, which is how it got its name, and it still looks ready for a love song.
card.stand_here: Walk to the Paseo Chabuca Granda, next to the Hermitage of Barranco, then stand about 35 m west of the Puente de los Suspiros, at the phone icon on the map. Face east and the bridge is right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x. If the whole bridge won't fit, tap 0.5x. Go to 2x or higher when you want a close-up of the wooden railings.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the bridge deck up with a horizontal line so it looks nice and level.
card.best_time: Afternoon is the friendly time. You're facing east, so the sun is behind you and lights up the front of the bridge. In the morning you're looking towards the sun, so the bridge can look dark. Tap the bridge and slide it brighter.
card.selfie_here: If the bridge is open, try the Puente de los Suspiros at either entrance, including the Jr. Batallón 271 side. Use the front camera, tap 0.5x, and keep the bridge over your shoulder. It works for group selfies too.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sloping cobbled path below the bridge (Bajada de los Baños) and shoot upward from a low angle, so the whole bridge fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge was closed in 2023 after damage to a neighbouring building, and reconstruction was announced, so check the official site before you go. Keep to well-lit routes and avoid walking alone after dark.
card.challenge: Get one shot with the deck perfectly level on the gridline and the railings leading the eye straight along the bridge. Bonus points if nobody wanders into it.
card.good_to_know: The bridge opened on 14 February 1876 and was destroyed in the War of the Pacific in 1881. In 1960 the composer Chabuca Granda dedicated a waltz to it, and there's a monument to her nearby. It was restored and reopened in December 2014.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the Paseo Chabuca Granda, next to the Hermitage of Barranco, then stand about 35 m west of the Puente de los Suspiros, at the phone icon on the map. Face east and the bridge is right in front of you.

selfie_spots.detail: at the two entrance ends of the wooden bridge, Jr. Batallón 271 side and the opposite end
selfie_spots.why: Tierras Vivas says the whole bridge works for group shots and selfies when you shoot from either end.

selfie_research.safety: Keep to well-lit routes and avoid walking alone after dark (Travelpander, https://travelpander.com/bridge-of-sighs-lima-peru/).
selfie_research.notes: Only one selfie spot is backed by a page that places the visitor with the bridge behind them; the entrance wording comes from a Google Translate proxy of the Tierras Vivas page. The 'ask someone' spot is the same page's low-angle suggestion, and the Bajada de Baños description comes from Peru Spirit. Two other candidates were found but not confirmed for a bridge-behind selfie: a sea-view gazebo on a side path (Tierras Vivas) and the start of the staircase where people photograph the 'Hogar de un suspiro' mural (a Wanderlog review). No page mentioned selfie stick or tripod rules. Sources disagree on the bridge's length (one review says about 40 feet, another says about 44 metres in a Wikimedia file), so I left length out.

card.hook: Picture a staircase that tips off the edge of Barranco and runs downhill between walls of colourful murals, with a wooden bridge hanging over the top. You won't need to hunt for a good photo here.
card.stand_here: Stand at the upper, Barranco-side end of the Puente de los Suspiros, on the wooden deck. Face down the ravine so the mural-lined steps fall away toward the sea with a bit of the bridge in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the bridge, the steps and the murals into one shot. Switch to 1x for a calmer view of the path, then 2x (if your phone has it) to pick out a single mural or a stretch of steps.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, let the line of the steps lead the eye downhill with the bridge to one side, and keep your phone level so the steps don't lean.
card.best_time: Earlier or later in the day usually means softer light and fewer people on the narrow steps, though it's worth checking the light when you get there. If you're at the footbridge at the bottom, sunset is said to be a favourite time.
card.selfie_here: Walk a little way down the cobbled Bajada to the mural stretch just under the Bridge of Sighs, and use the front camera with the colourful wall behind you. Try 0.5x and hold the phone a bit higher so the murals and steps both fit over your shoulder. The pedestrian bridge at the bottom, where the Bajada meets the beach road, also works, with the stepped path behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Avenida San Martín overpass while you stand on the Bajada below, so they can frame you with the steps and Calle La Ermita around you.
card.rules_and_safety: The stairs are steep in places, so save some energy for the walk back up. The lower section near the coast is fenced and roofed, which may limit open-air views down there.
card.challenge: Take one shot from the bridge, then one from inside the Bajada, and see if anyone can guess they're the same place.
card.good_to_know: Bajada de Baños is a stepped pedestrian path that drops from the edge of Barranco down a ravine toward the sea. Its walls are covered in murals, and the Puente de los Suspiros is the wooden footbridge at the top. There's also a lookout beside the bridge with a wider view over the coast.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the upper, Barranco-side end of the Puente de los Suspiros, on the wooden deck. Face down the ravine so the mural-lined steps fall away toward the sea with a bit of the bridge in the frame.

selfie_spots.detail: on the footbridge where the Bajada reaches the beach road, with the stepped path in the frame behind you
selfie_spots.why: A guide calls this bridge a popular photo spot, especially at sunset, and it sits at the lower end of the Bajada.

Some pages describe Bajada de Baños as a hiking trail, while others describe a cobbled street down to the beach; the street description matches the photo sources better. card.hook: Picture a marble statue in the foreground, a old church glowing behind it, and you haven't walked more than a few steps. That's the trick of this little park.
card.stand_here: Head for the fountain and pergola stage at the centre of Parque Municipal de Barranco, about 56 m to the north-west, roughly a minute's walk. Face the statues that look toward the Iglesia Santísima Cruz, so the church sits behind them.
card.zoom: Start at 0.5x to get the stage, fountain and church in one frame, then switch to 1x for the fountain with the buildings behind it. For the statue and cherub details, try 2x to 5x, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put a statue on one of the lines with the church behind it, then tap the statue and slide it a little darker so the white marble doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go at sunset or early morning, when the soft light brings out the carving and the old façades.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the edge of the central pond by the naiads' fountain, with the Venus statue on its water mirror behind you. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a bit low so the statue shows over your shoulder. The pergola stage also makes a good backdrop: stand under or beside it with the structure filling the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It looks like an open public park, but check the official site before you go for any opening times or restrictions.
card.challenge: Find a cherub, then frame it so the church or the library sits right behind it.
card.good_to_know: The park has lawns, trees, marble statues, cherub figures, the naiads' fountain and the Candelabro Barberini, all close together. The Venus figure on the water mirror is nicknamed La Donaide. The Iglesia Santísima Cruz and the municipal library stand around it, so old façades are always in the background.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the fountain and pergola stage at the centre of Parque Municipal de Barranco, about 56 m to the north-west, roughly a minute's walk. Face the statues that look toward the Iglesia Santísima Cruz, so the church sits behind them.

selfie_spots.why: A photo-spot guide lists this pergola stage as one of the park's picture spots, so it is a likely backdrop for a selfie.

The selfie spots are named by photo-guide lists of park features (pergola stage, naiad fountain, Candelabro Barberini), not by exact positions, so the exact spot to stand is my inference from those features and should be checked on the ground. No page mentioned selfie-stick or tripod rules, and no safety point about the park itself was stated; one reviewer said they felt unsafe going up the Bajada de Baños steps alone, which is outside the park and is a personal impression, so I omitted it.

card.hook: Pointing your phone at a photography museum feels a bit like bringing a sandwich to a restaurant, but go on, do it. MATE's frontage and street make nice clean frames.
card.stand_here: Start on Jirón Octavio Cavero, at the phone icon on the map, about 50 m north-east of the subject. Face south-west and the museum is ahead of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for your main view. If the street feels narrow and you can't step back, drop to 0.5x. Then try 2x, if your phone has it, for the entrance or signs.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the building up with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Daytime is easiest for outside shots. Early morning or late afternoon often gives softer light and fewer people. Check the official site for opening arrangements before you go.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera and switch to 0.5x so the museum fits over your shoulder. Hold the phone a little higher than your face, and keep the museum's frontage or sign in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Personal, non-commercial photos are generally allowed inside MATE, but follow the museum's rules and etiquette. Selfie sticks may need special permission, and one guide says the museum asks visitors not to use them, so leave yours in your bag. They can be a hazard in crowded rooms.
card.challenge: Take three shots: one wide to show where you are, one at 1x for the main view, and one close-up of a door, sign or texture that catches your eye.
card.good_to_know: MATE is the Museo Mario Testino, named after the photographer, and it sits in Barranco. Its name and purpose make it a natural 'I was here' picture for your trip album. Entry may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site first.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Start on Jirón Octavio Cavero, at the phone icon on the map, about 50 m north-east of the subject. Face south-west and the museum is ahead of you.

Pedro de Osma 409 on most pages, but Washington Post lists Pedro de Osma 421 beside the MATE entry, so check the door number on a map. Bushop's guide says MATE is closed Mondays. The tripod and selfie-stick rules conflict in tone: one page says special permission may be needed, another says the museum requests that they not be used.

card.hook: Statues stand guard at the door of an old colonial mansion that's now a shop, and they make a great start to your Barranco wander. Dedalo is spot number 6 on the map, and it's a quick, easy photo stop.
card.stand_here: Head to the phone icon near Pasaje Tacna, about 25 m south of Dedalo, and face north. From here you get a clear first look at the whole thing before you move closer.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view. Switch to 0.5x only if you can't fit everything in, and keep Dedalo away from the edges so it doesn't stretch. Then walk closer and use zoom 2x for details like signs and textures.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put Dedalo on a line or crossing point, and keep your phone level so the vertical lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters outdoor subjects and avoids harsh shadows. On a bright, overcast day, colours and details often look even and easy to photograph.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the statues at the entrance of Dédalo (Sáenz Peña 295), with the colonial-house facade behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if you want the doorway and building to fit in with you.
card.rules_and_safety: Access and rules for getting closer aren't confirmed, so check the official site before you go. Be polite to other people while you take your pictures.
card.challenge: Get one shot with Dedalo on a gridline crossing and nobody walking through the frame. Be patient, or take a few in a row and pick the winner.
card.good_to_know: Dedalo is spot number 6 on the Barranco map. The building is an old colonial mansion turned into a shop. Wipe your phone's camera with a soft cloth first, because pockets and bags leave a film that softens photos.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the phone icon near Pasaje Tacna, about 25 m south of Dedalo, and face north. From here you get a clear first look at the whole thing before you move closer.

selfie_spots.detail: in front of the statues guarding the shop's entrance, with the colonial-house facade behind you
selfie_spots.why: Statues guard the entrance to this old colonial mansion-turned-shop, so the doorway and building make a ready-made backdrop for a solo selfie.

Its address is written as both 'Jirón' and 'Paseo/Pasaje' Sáenz Peña across sources; the same street is meant. A Tripadvisor listing for the Barranco paseo mentions cliff-edge caution, but that applies to the paseo's ocean end, not the Dédalo frontage, so I left the safety field empty.

card.hook: Ever tried to fit a 187 m building into one phone photo? At MAC Lima in Barranco, that's the whole game, and it's more fun than it sounds.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the Museum of Contemporary Art (MAC Lima), where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the building, then walk back as far as the surroundings allow until you can see the full width.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to grab the whole building. Switch to 1x for one natural-looking section, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for entrances, signs and textures.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's long horizontal edges with them, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the building. If the sky looks washed out, tap the building and drag the slider to make it a little darker.
card.selfie_here: Head into the park grounds and stand beside the pond with the museum behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the building over your shoulder. The big outdoor sculptures on the grounds could make a fun backdrop too.
card.rules_and_safety: Check the official site before you go for entry rules and whether photography is allowed inside the exhibition rooms.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with some sky, then wait for a stranger to stroll through the frame so everyone can see how huge the building is.
card.good_to_know: MAC Lima opened formally in late January 2013, in a building designed by Peruvian architect Frederick Cooper Llosa. It stands on the old Barranco Zoo site, which closed in 1970, and the building now sits on top of the zoo's old artificial lake. In December 2024 it opened Contemporáneo 1, a show of its permanent collection.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the Museum of Contemporary Art (MAC Lima), where the phone icon on the map sits. Face the building, then walk back as far as the surroundings allow until you can see the full width.

selfie_spots.name: Pond in the outdoor park of the Museum of Contemporary Art (MAC Lima)
selfie_spots.detail: in the park grounds beside the pond, with the museum building behind you
selfie_spots.why: A visitor guide names the exterior park area with its pond as a good photo area, and it is the museum's main outdoor setting.

card.hook: Picture a pink-and-yellow church with no roof, sitting right at the edge of a cliff with the ocean behind it. That's the Ermita in Barranco, and its weathered, empty shell is exactly why it looks so good on your phone.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plazuela Chabuca Granda, in front of the church beside the entrance steps. The church lies to the south-west of you, so face south-west and keep the whole building in the frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the full facade with the cliff edge and ocean behind it. Tap 0.5x if you want the plaza and entrance steps in too, then try 2x or higher (depends on your phone) for close-ups of the textured walls.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the facade up with the vertical lines so the walls stand straight.
card.best_time: Go at sunset on a clear day, when the colours are at their best. Between roughly May and October the coastal mist can flatten the sky, so a clear evening is worth waiting for.
card.selfie_here: Climb the stairway up to the church, turn around so the church front is behind you, and keep the Plazuela Chabuca Granda off to one side. Use the front camera, hold it a little above eye level, and try 0.5x if your phone has it to squeeze more church into the shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the plaza, near the Chabuca Granda statue, and shoot from the plaza side so the whole facade fits, while you pose on the steps.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is closed to visitors, so photograph the outside only. If you go down the Bajada de los Baños for a different view, it's steep and can be busy, so keep your phone close and watch your footing.
card.challenge: Take two shots of the same church: one big, with the whole building and the ocean, and one tiny, filling the frame with nothing but crumbly pink-and-yellow wall. Then see which one your friends like better.
card.good_to_know: The Ermita began in the mid-18th century as a modest chapel for fishermen and travellers. Local legend says it marks where Barranco began, after two lost fishermen were guided ashore by the light of a cross. The church was burned in 1881 during the War of the Pacific and rebuilt the following year, and it has been closed since the 1974 earthquake.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plazuela Chabuca Granda, in front of the church beside the entrance steps. The church lies to the south-west of you, so face south-west and keep the whole building in the frame.

selfie_spots.why: A traveler's photo caption describes the staircase leading to the church, and a Tripadvisor reviewer notes the plaza sits to the right of those steps, so the church is the backdrop.

card.hook: Be honest: the statues alone won't blow you away, and plenty of visitors say so. The magic is the whole scene, with a singer, a horseman and the Bridge of Sighs all in one spot.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Puente de los Suspiros, on the Bajada de Baños side, and face back toward the Plazuela Chabuca Granda. Check when you arrive that the statues show clearly. If they're hard to spot, step onto the plazuela side instead.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the bridge, the plazuela and both statues into one frame. Then try 1x for a natural look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Chabuca Granda or the horse from a distance.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, line the bridge rails up with them so they look straight, and put the statues on one of the thirds.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon is best, when the light is softer and the shadows on the figures aren't so harsh. If the sky is very bright, tap the statue and drag the slider down to make it a bit darker, so the figures don't turn into dark shapes.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x so you fit in with the statues over your shoulder. Hold the phone a little higher and check the corners for bins and signs before you tap.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the steps of Iglesia La Ermita and shoot down toward the statues while you stand beside them. Chabuca Granda is on the left as you go down.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an open public plazuela beside the bridge, with no access restrictions.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with the bridge rails perfectly straight, then one close-up of the horseman, and see which one your friends like better.
card.good_to_know: The statue of Chabuca Granda stands next to an equestrian statue of José Antonio de Lavalle y García, the man her song "José Antonio" is about. Granda spent part of her childhood on a ranch on the Bajada de los Baños, near the bridge, and dedicated a song to the bridge in 1960. The sculptor was Fausto Jaulis from Ayacucho, and the monument was inaugurated on 24 October 1992.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Puente de los Suspiros, on the Bajada de Baños side, and face back toward the Plazuela Chabuca Granda. Check when you arrive that the statues show clearly. If they're hard to spot, step onto the plazuela side instead.

The monument's coordinates match your position (Wikipedia gives 12°08′56″S 77°01′22″W). The Plazuela sits next to the La Ermita steps and in front of the Bridge of Sighs (Komoot). card.hook: The best move at this church is to walk away from it. Barranco's central park is right in front, and every step back gives you more church and more leafy frame.
card.stand_here: Stand in Parque Municipal de Barranco, across the park from the church front. The church is to the north-west, about 1 minute on foot, so turn round and face north-west.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole front and the bell tower. Try 0.5x only if you want lots of trees and park, and keep the church away from the edges so it doesn't stretch. Then go to 2x to pick out the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines, put the church in the middle third and use the lines to keep the tower standing straight.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the park. Pick a time when the sun isn't right behind the church, so the front is evenly lit.
card.selfie_here: Head to the park side facing the church in Parque Municipal de Barranco and stand with the church behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and keep the church away from the edges so it stays in your picture. Use 0.5x if your front camera has it.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the park, across the square, and frame the church front while you stand in the picture with the church behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The church is a working place of worship, so keep a respectful distance from anyone going in. If you want to go inside, check current opening hours and any festival-related street closures first.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with trees framing the top, then one tight shot of the tower, and see if you can get the tower perfectly upright in both.
card.good_to_know: The Iglesia de la Santísima Cruz stands directly in front of Barranco's central park. The park is a public space, so people keep wandering through, and if someone walks into your shot, just wait a moment. A Live Photo can help when the park is busy.
